summary:
Burundi criminalizes sexual relations with a person of the same sex under Article 567 of the Penal Code. The provision was passed on 22 November 2008 and took effect on 22 April 2009. It applies to conduct by both men and women. The prescribed penalty is three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 francs. Such conduct was not criminalized before that date.

Article 29 of the Constitution of Burundi prohibits same-sex marriage. Burundi does not recognize same-sex marriages or civil unions.

Enforcement reflects a national pattern of arrests for same-sex conduct that ended without conviction for consensual adult conduct, with one conviction where a homosexuality charge accompanied admission of child rape. Police in Bujumbura detained a man in 2009 and sought money for release before advocacy secured his freedom. A 2014 case involving two men in Karuzi Province was dropped after three days for lack of evidence. Two women detained in 2012 were briefly held and released. A court in 2016 sentenced a 15-year-old who admitted rape of a seven-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality.

In December 2023 President Evariste Ndayishimiye said gay sex was like choosing Satan and that gay people found in Burundi should be taken to stadiums and stoned. He repeated the call for stoning homosexuals in January 2024.

Human Rights Watch condemned the January 2024 call and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. LGBTQ people in Burundi reported terror after the remarks. The Iteka League, operating in exile, described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as a real license to kill them.

United States State Department human rights reports for 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gay and lesbian or LGBT persons under the criminal framework. The 2015 report records arrests and harassment of LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
General human rights conditions reported alongside LGBT discrimination indicate a high-risk enforcement environment. The 2015 United States report describes extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and media shutdowns during a national crisis.

Earlier foreign reporting recorded similar coercive conditions. The 2010 report listed security-force killings, torture and harsh prison conditions among common abuses. The 2012 report documented torture, extrajudicial executions and prolonged pretrial detention.
localsOnly:
Domestic LGBT organizing operates under constraint. The Iteka League functions in exile. Members of two LGBTQ associations spoke only on condition of anonymity when describing the presidential remarks as a license to kill.

The 2016 conviction combining rape of a minor and homosexuality was imposed by the High Court of Cibitoke Province. Police practice in the 2009 Bujumbura detention included seeking money in exchange for release.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the inventory: rules on legal gender recognition and identity documents for trans persons, entry and visa treatment, airport or detention screening practices, access to gender-affirming care, bathroom or facilities rules, and hate-crime protections.

Unresolved whether routine policing distinguishes consensual adult same-sex conduct from other charges, beyond the documented arrests that ended without conviction and the single 2016 case combining homosexuality with admitted child rape.
